# Book Pages 136–283 # Constituted Text Only; Critical Apparatus Removed ## Part 1. Sarga and Pratisarga | Chapter 2
Manu said: [Tell me] of the origin and the dissolution, as well as the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras, the history of the dynasties, and the detailed extent of the universe.
He taught the rules for the gift of dharma, the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha),
the classification of social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), and likewise that which is known as iṣṭāpūrta.
The installation of deities and whatever else exists on earth—all that you ought to explain in detail according to the Dharma! || 24 ||
Matsya said:
At the end of the time of the great dissolution, this world was composed of darkness; it was as if fast asleep, inconceivable, unknown, and devoid of defining characteristics. || 25 ||
The world—both the stationary and the moving—is unknowable and unperceived;
from that [proceeds] the self-existent, unmanifest source of those who perform meritorious deeds. (26)

Manifesting all this, the dispeller of darkness appeared—he who is beyond the senses, superior to the manifest, atomic yet greater than the great, eternal, known as Nārāyaṇa; he alone shone forth by himself. || 27 ||
He who, desiring to emit the manifold world by meditating upon his own body, first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. || 28 ||
That very [substance] became a great egg, composed of gold and silver, possessing a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns, which took a thousand years to form. || 29 ||
Having entered within himself by his own power, the one of great splendor, born of his own self, once again attained the state of Viṣṇu through that pervasive pervasion. || 30 ||
Within that, this Lord Sūrya came into being in the beginning;
and because he was the primordial source, Āditya became Brahmā while reciting the Veda. || 31 ||
He made the two halves of that eggshell into heaven and earth;
he created all the directions and the eternal sky in their midst. || 32 ||
Then the mountains, with Meru as their chief, became his placenta;
and that which was the outer membrane (ulba) became a mass of clouds together with a circle of lightning. || 33 ||
The rivers, the channels of the cosmic egg, as well as the ancestors and the Manus,
and these seven oceans— all of which arise from within the waters—
are filled with various jewels such as salt, sugarcane juice, wine, and the like. || 34 ||
O subduer of enemies, that god Prajāpati became desirous of creating;
and from his vital energy (tejas), Mārtaṇḍa was born there. || 35 ||

Because he was born from a dead egg, he is celebrated as Mārtaṇḍa. That form of the Great-Souled One which consists of the quality of passion (rajas) became the four-faced Lord, the Grandfather of the worlds. || 36 ||
Know that by whom this entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, was created—that is the nature of Rajas; it is declared to be the Great Being (Mahat). || 36 ||
## Section One: Primary Creation and Secondary Creation | Chapter 3 Manu said:
Why did the Grandfather of the worlds attain the state of having four faces?
But how did Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, create the worlds? || 1 ||
Matsya said:
First, the Grandfather performed austerities for the sake of the immortals;
thereupon the Vedas appeared, complete with their limbs, sub-limbs, word-order, and phonetic arrangements. || 2 ||
The Purāṇa, composed by Brahmā at the beginning of all scriptures,
is eternal, consisting of sound, meritorious, and extends to one billion verses.
And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths, along with Mīmāṃsā and the sciences of Nyāya, together with the eight means of valid cognition (pramāṇas). || 4 ||

For him, who was devoted to the study of the Vedas and desirous of offspring, there were the Mānasas; because they were indeed created by his mind as a previous creation, they are therefore called Mānasas. || 5 ||
Marīci appeared first; after him was the venerable seer Atri; then Aṅgiras appeared, and immediately after him was Pulastya. || 6 ||
Then indeed one named Pulaha was born; from him Kratu was born;
then Pracetas was his son, and Vasiṣṭha was born again. || 7 ||
In that same manner, Bhṛgu became his son, and Nārada also appeared shortly thereafter;
Brahmā thus procreated these ten sages as his mind-born sons.
Now I shall describe the bodily [progeny] of Prajāpati who were deprived of their mothers:
from the right thumb, Dakṣa was born as Prajāpati. || 9 ||
From the space between her breasts Dharma was born; from her heart, the flower-weaponed god of love;
from the middle of her brows, Anger arose; and Greed was produced from her lower lip. Delusion emerged from her intellect, and Arrogance sprang from her ego.
O King, joy issued from his throat, death from his eyes;
Bharata emerged from the middle of his hand, and from that, the son of Brahmā was born. || 11 ||
O King, these are the nine sons, and the tenth is again a daughter;
she is renowned as Aṅgajā, the tenth daughter of Brahmā. || 12 ||
Manu said: Regarding that which has been proclaimed—that delusion arose from the intellect (buddhi)—egoism (ahaṃkāra) is traditionally known as anger; what, then, is called "intellect"? || 13 ||
Matsya said:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas);
their state of equilibrium is proclaimed as Prakṛti. || 14 ||
Some call it Pradhāna; others have sung of it as the Unmanifest (avyakta);
this very thing creates the world of beings and transforms it. || 15 ||
From the qualities being agitated, three gods were born:
one single form with three portions—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. || 16 ||
From the Pradhāna, which is subject to modification, the Mahat-tattva is produced;
it is called "Mahat" because from it the manifestation (khyāti) of the worlds always arises. || 17 ||

And from the Great One (mahat) arises ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), which increases human pride; from that [arise] the five senses, which I shall describe as being under the control of the intellect (buddhi), and likewise others that arise under the control of karma. || 18 ||
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose; and in due order, the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech—this is the summary of the sense faculties. || 19 ||
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; and excretion, pleasure, grasping, movement, and speech—these are their functions. || 20 ||

The mind is the eleventh among them, endowed with the qualities of action and cognition. Since the wise hold that the subtle components of the sense organs resort to it as their form, the body is therefore traditionally called *tanmātra*.
Due to its connection with the body, the individual soul (jīva) is also called "embodied" by the wise. || 22 ||
The mind, impelled by the desire to create, undergoes transformation and produces the creation;
from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), space arose, having sound as its essential quality. || 23 ||
From the transformation of space, wind arose, possessing the qualities of sound and touch;
and from the subtle element of touch belonging to wind, fire then emerged. || 24 ||
Through its transformation, that [fire] possessed three qualities and was endowed with sound, touch, and form;
from the transformation of fire, O King, water arose, possessing four qualities. || 25 ||

Earth, which is produced from the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra), consists primarily of the quality of taste; however, earth arose from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) and is endowed with five qualities. || 26 ||
That [earth] possesses the quality of smell as its primary attribute; this intellect (buddhi) is more exalted [than the elements].
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, enjoys that which has been prepared by these [elements and intellects]. || 27 ||
Even that individual soul is said by the wise to be under the power of the Lord’s will.
Thus, the twenty-sixth principle is here declared by men to be the body. || 28 ||
And because its nature consists of enumeration, it is called Sāṃkhya by Kapila and others.
Having made this [system] the essence of reality, the Creator produced the world. || 29 ||
Having fixed the Sāvitrī mantra in his heart for the purpose of creating the worlds, he remained steadfast;
then, as he was reciting it, [the mantra] pierced through his stainless body.
He made one half female in form and the other half male in form;
she is known as Śatarūpā and is also called Sāvitrī. || 31 ||
Then, O scorcher of foes, Sarasvatī became Gāyatrī and Brahmāṇī;
thereafter, he conceived her as his own daughter, born from his own body. || 32 ||
Upon seeing her, the Lord Prajāpati was pained and afflicted by the arrows of love; he exclaimed, "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what beauty! || 33 ||
Then those led by Vasiṣṭha cried out, "Sister!";
Brahmā saw nothing at all except for the sight of her face. || 34 ||
"Aho! What beauty! Aho! What beauty! he said again and again;
then he gazed once more at her as she bowed low in salutation. || 35 ||
Then that woman of excellent complexion circumambulated her father out of a desire to behold his form, as he was ashamed before his sons. || 36 ||
Then the right face appeared, with pale cheeks; thereafter, the western face arose, its lips quivering with wonder. || 37 ||
Afterwards, his left [side] became the fourth, afflicted by the arrows of desire;
then another arose for him in that same way through the intensity of his passion. (38)
As she was flying up into the sky out of curiosity to see it, [he recalled] that most terrible penance which he had performed for the purpose of creation. || 39 ||
All that vanished through his desire for the arrival of his own son.
Consequently, a fifth face appeared on the upper part of that wise one's head;
and the Lord covered that face with manifesting matted locks. || 40 ||
Then Brahmā spoke to those sons born from his own self:
"Create offspring on all sides, including gods, asuras, and humans! (41)
Thus addressed, they all then created various kinds of progeny.
When they had departed for the sake of creation, [he beheld] her, bowed down in salutation.
The Soul of the Universe married the faultless Śatarūpā; that omnipresent Lord, overcome with intense passion,
dallied with her in the interior of a lotus-blossom palace, though she was filled with modesty.
For as long as a hundred divine years— as is the case for any other ordinary person—
after that great length of time, a son named Manu was born to her.
He is known as Svāyambhuva; we have heard that he is called Virāj.
Because of the commonality of his form and qualities, he is termed Adhipuruṣa. || 45 ||
Where those many Vairājas were born, firm in their vows—the highly fortunate sons of Svayambhū, seven groups of seven each, as well as others. || 46 ||
All those beginning with Svārociṣa were equal in nature to Brahmā;
likewise were those headed by Auttami, of whom you are now the seventh.
**Chapter 4: Primary and Secondary Creation** **Section 1: Sarga and Pratisarga** Manu said:
"O Lord, this arrival of your own offspring is indeed most painful!"
How did the Lotus-born One not incur fault through this action? || 1 ||
And how did mutual understanding arise among those of the same lineage?
O Lord, sever my doubt regarding the marriages of their sons! || 2 ||
Matsya said:
This divine primordial creation, however, arose from the quality of rajas;
it possesses senses beyond the reach of the senses, and likewise its embodied beings possess bodies beyond the reach of the senses.
O King, consisting of divine splendor and arising from divine knowledge, she cannot indeed be fully described by mortals with their eyes of flesh. || 4 ||
Just as serpents know the path of snakes, the sky of birds, and the divine ones of the divine, so it is for those who are divine themselves, and not for mere mortals. || 5 ||

For the gods do not bestow auspicious or inauspicious fruits based on what ought to be done or what ought not to be done; therefore, O Indra among kings, it is not beneficial for men to deliberate upon that. || 6 ||
Furthermore: The four-faced one is the presiding deity of all the Vedas;
likewise, Gāyatrī is declared to be a constituent limb of Brahmā. || 7 ||
Whether formless or even possessing form, they declare that to be a couple. Where the venerable Viriñci is, there is the goddess Sarasvatī; wherever Bhāratī is, there indeed is Prajāpati. || 8 ||
Just as heat is never seen anywhere without its shadow, even so Gāyatrī does not leave the side of Brahmā. || 9 ||
Brahmā is remembered as the mass of the Vedas, and Sāvitrī is established upon him;
therefore, O Lord, there would be no fault whatsoever in the Lord’s approaching Sāvitrī. || 10 ||
Nevertheless, in ancient times, Prajāpati Brahmā became bowed down with shame; because of his approaching his own daughter, he cursed the flower-armed god of love. || 11 ||
"Since my mind has been agitated by your arrows that overwhelm me, therefore Rudra shall soon reduce your body to ashes. || 12 ||
Then Kāmadeva propitiated the Four-faced One:
"O Giver of Honor, you ought not to curse me here without cause! (13)
"O Four-faced One, I have been created by you in such a manner that I cause the agitation of the senses in all embodied beings. || 14 ||
"O Lord, you yourself previously stated that the mind of both women and men must be diligently agitated by me everywhere and at all times without hesitation. (15)
Therefore, O Lord, I have been cursed by you despite being innocent;
O Blessed One, show me favor so that I may regain my own body once again! (16)
Brahmā said: When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, there will be one named Rāma, born of the lineage of the Yādavas, who, as a mortal, shall rely upon my own strength and power.
Having descended to destroy the path of the gods, he will dwell in Dvārakā;
at that time, you shall become the son of his brother, who is equal to him. || 18 ||
Thus, having attained a body and enjoyed all pleasures without exception,
he was thereafter born as the son of the king of Vatsa at the end of the Bharata dynasty.
Having attained sovereignty over the Vidyādharas and all manner of pleasures through the Dharma until the dissolution of the world, you shall come into my presence. || 20 ||
Thus, endowed with both curse and favor, the flower-armed god, possessed of both grief and joy, departed as he had come. || 21 ||
Manu said:
Who was this person called Yadu, in whose lineage the birth of Kāma occurred;
and how, and for what reason, was the flower-armed god burnt by Rudra? || 22 ||
In the lineage of Bharata, who was there and what creation occurred in ancient times?
Explain all of this from the very beginning, for I have a doubt. || 23 ||
Matsya said: She who was born from half of his body, Gāyatrī, the expounder of Brahman;
she who is the mother of Manu, O Goddess, Śatarūpā, possessing a hundred faculties. || 24 ||
Rati, Manas, Tapas, Buddhi, Mahān, Diś, and Samṛbhrama;
from her, Śatarūpā gave birth to these seven sons. || 25 ||
Of those mind-born sons of his, Marīci and the others, this world consisting of all knowledge was formerly the portion belonging to him. || 26 ||
Then he created Vāmadeva, who bears the excellent trident, and the omnipresent Sanatkumāra, the progenitor even of the ancient ones. || 27 ||
The blessed Vāmadeva, however, created the twice-born from his mouth;
he created the kṣatriyas from his arms, and the vaiśyas and śūdras from his thighs and feet. || 28 ||
In the beginning, he created lightning, thunderbolts, and clouds, as well as red-hued rainbows;
thereafter, he created the Vedic meters and Parjanya. || 29 ||
Then the Lord again created eighty-four crores of Sādhyas, three-eyed and free from old age and death. || 30 ||
Vāma created those immortals, but he was restrained by Brahmā:
"A creation such as this, devoid of old age and death, must not come to be! || 31 ||
That which consists of both the auspicious and the inauspicious is alone praised as creation.
Because he remained thus at the beginning of creation, he therefore became Sthāṇu (the Immovable).

## Section 3: The Manvantaras | A. (Kūrma Purāṇa 51.1–36; Viṣṇu Purāṇa III.1.5–47) I shall relate to you correctly and in their proper sequence all those *manvantaras* that have passed and those yet to come in this world. || 1 ||
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Manu Svārociṣa;
likewise Auttami, Tamasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa. || 2 ||
These six Manus have passed away; now, however, it is the son of Ravi (the Sun).
This is Vaivasvata, whose seventh *antara* is currently underway. || 3 ||
I have thus described to you the intermediate period of the Svāyambhuva Kalpa at its beginning,
as well as the gods and the ṛṣis exactly as they were. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the period of Svārociṣa Manu.
He [described] correctly the lords of the Manvantaras, the divine sages, and their sons;
and the Pārāvatas and Tuṣitas were the gods in the Svārociṣa interval. || 5 ||
There was a lord of the gods named Vipaścit, the crusher of the Asuras;
likewise Ūrjas, Stambha, Prāṇa, Dattoli, and Ṛṣabha.
Niśvara and Urvarīvan were the seven sages there, while Caitra, Kimpuruṣa, and others were the sons of Svārociṣa. || 7 ||
This second intermediate period has been described; now hear about the supreme one! And in the third intermediate period, the Manu named Auttami shall indeed appear. || 8 ||
There, the lord of the gods, the subduer of enemies, was Suśānti;
likewise, the Pratardanas were Sudhāman, Satya, and Śiva. || 9 ||
These five groups of twelve are known as the Vaśavartins:
Rajo, Gātra, and Ardhabāhu; and among them were the sons of Vasiṣṭha—Savana and Anagha. Thus, there were seven Saptarṣis.
Sutapās and Śakra—these were [the gods]. The seven Saptarṣis were Aja, Paraśu, Divya, and the others. The sons of Auttami Manu were the Surūpas and the Haris;
these were the gods during the interval (antara) of Tāmasa Manu.
There were twenty-seven groups of truthful and wise men; Śibi was their Indra, characterized by the performance of a hundred sacrifices,
and he became a devotee of Śaṅkara, as did those who were the seven ṛṣis.
He was devoted to the worship of Mahādeva. In that regard, hear my names: || 12 ||
Jyotirdhāman, Pṛthu, Kāvya, Caitra, Agni, Vanaka, and Pivara—these were the seven sages during that interval as well. || 13 ||
From him were born Khyāti, Śātahaya, Jānujaṅgha, and others;
these were the sons of Tāmasa, kings of exceedingly great strength. || 13 ||
And in the fifth [manvantara], O Maitreya, there was one known by the name Raivata;
Manu was the sovereign and Indra was there, so hear now of the gods in that interval: || 14 ||
Amitābha, Ābhūtarajas, Vaikuṇṭha, and Sumedhas—these are the fourteen groups of gods there, fourteen for each. || 15 ||
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedaśrī, likewise Ūrdhvabāhu,
Vedabāhu, Sudhāman, and the great sage Parjanya—
these were the seven ṛṣis, O Brahmin, during that Raivata Manvantara. || 16 ||
Balabandhu was to be honored, as were his sons, Satyaka and the others;
they became kings of great prowess, O best of sages. (16)
Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa, and Raivata—these four Manus likewise belong to the lineage of Priyavrata. || 17 ||
O Priyavrata, by propitiating Viṣṇu through austerity, that royal sage obtained these lords of the Manvantaras born from his own lineage. || 17 ||
In the sixth Manvantara, there was likewise a Manu named Cākṣuṣa;
Indrānuja (Manojava) was the Indra; now learn from me also about the gods: || 18 ||
The Ādyas, Prasūtas, Bhavyas, Pṛthugas, Divaukasas, Mahānubhāvas, and Lekhas—these five groups each consist of eight classes. || 19 ||
Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Uttama, Madhu, Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu—these were the seven auspicious ṛṣis. || 20 ||
Ūru, Pūru, and others headed by Śatadyumna—sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu who possessed great strength—became lords of the earth. || 20 ||
O sage, the son of Vivasvat, the highly effulgent Śrāddhadeva, that wise Manu is currently presiding over the seventh interval (antara). || 21 ||
O great sage Maitreya, the gods beginning with the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, as well as Puraṃdara, the lord of the thirty-three, are present here. || 22 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja—these seven became the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). || 23 ||
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, the renowned Nariṣyanta, and Nābhāgodita. || 23 ||
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Vasumān, world-renowned—these were the nine righteous sons of Manu Vaivasvata. || 23 ||

The incomparable power of Viṣṇu, abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva), is established in the maintenance of the world; kings are its manifestations, as are all the inhabitants of heaven throughout all the Manvantaras. He presides over them as their divinity.
Then again, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, that very god was born in Tuṣitā together with the Tuṣita gods as Ajita. || 26 ||
Furthermore, in the interval between Uttama and Tāmasa, he was indeed Tuṣita;
in the Satya Manvantara, he became Satya, together with the best of gods who were likewise truthful. || 27 ||
And when the interval of Tāmasa had indeed arrived once again, Hari himself became Hari once more together with the Haris in the womb of Haryā. || 28 ||
In the Raivata interval as well, in the period of Sambhūti, Hari, the best of gods, was born from the mind; that Hari, the supreme deity, was born together with the mind-born gods. || 29 ||
And during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, that Puruṣottama Vaikuṇṭha was born in the city of Vikuṇṭhā together with the Vaikuṇṭha deities. || 30 ||
But when the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived, O twice-born one, Viṣṇu was born as Vāmana from Kaśyapa and Aditi. || 31 ||
By that Great-souled One, having conquered these worlds with three strides, the three realms were given to Purandara, cleared of all thorns. || 32 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, these were his seven bodies during the seven Manvantaras, by which the subjects were protected. || 33 ||
Since all this has been pervaded by the Great-Souled Vāmana, he is therefore remembered as Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter. || 34 ||
And all the gods, all human beings,
the seven seers, and those who are the sons of Manu,
as well as Indra, who has become the lord of the thirty-three gods—
But those are all the infinite manifestations of Viṣṇu. || 341 ||
**Chapter 3: The Manvantaras** **(Viṣṇu Purāṇa III.2.1–60)** Maitreya said:
"These seven manvantaras have indeed been described by you."
O brahmin-sage, you ought to tell me also of those that are yet to come! || 1 ||
Parāśara said: Saṃjñā, who was the daughter of Viśvakarman, became the wife of Sūrya;
O Sage, their offspring were indeed Manu, Yama, and Yamī. || 2 ||
But she, unable to endure her husband’s splendor, indeed assigned him shade;
she went to the forest herself for the sake of asceticism, while remaining devoted to the service of her husband. || 3 ||
Thinking, "This is a woman," Arka then begot upon Chāyā another son, Manu, along with Sanaiścara and Tapatī. || 4 ||
When Chāyā, filled with anger, pronounced a curse upon Yama, both Yama and Sūrya thought, "This is another [person], not she. || 5 ||
Then Vivasvat was informed by her of her dwelling in the forest;
with his vision of meditative concentration, he beheld that mare established in asceticism.
Then the two gods, the Aśvins, assuming the form of horses, begot Revanta upon her; and at the end of that seminal emission, the Sun-god [beheld him]. || 7 ||
Furthermore, the Lord Sun restored consciousness to her, and Viśvakarman performed the pacification of her radiance. || 8 ||
Having placed the sun upon his lathe, he diminished its brilliance;
yet he could not diminish the eighth part of that imperishable one.
O best of sages, that Vaiṣṇava splendor which had been severed from the sun by Viśvakarman fell blazing upon the earth. || 10 ||
With that splendor, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned Viṣṇu’s discus,
as well as Rudra’s trident and the palanquin of Dhanada.
Viśvakarman strengthened with that splendor all the weapons of Guha, of the gods, and of others as well. || 12 ||
He who was called the second Manu, the son of Chāyāsaṃjñā, was of the same caste (savarṇa) as his elder brother; therefore, he is called Sāvarṇi. || 13 ||
This is indeed the Manvantara of Sāvarṇika, following that one. Now, O highly fortunate one, listen to the eighth; I shall tell you of what is to come. || 14 ||
O Maitreya, he who will then be Manu Sāvarṇi, as well as the gods Sutapas, Amitābhas, and Mukhyas, shall then be the presiding deities. || 15 ||
The host of each of those gods consists of twenty well-performed ones.
O best of sages, I shall now also declare the future seven ṛṣis.
The radiant Gālava, Rāma, Kṛpa, and likewise the son of Droṇa;
my son, as well as Vyāsa, and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga as the seventh. || 17 ||
By the grace of Viṣṇu, O sinless one, Bali, the son of Virocana, who dwells within the netherworld, shall become their Indra. || 18 ||
Viraja, Arvarīvat, Nirmoha, and others likewise—these will be the sons of Sāvarṇa Manu, the lords of men. || 19 ||
O Maitreya, Dakṣasāvarṇi will be the ninth Manu; his sons will be of three kinds: the Pārās, the Marīcīgarbhas, and the Sudharmans.
At that time, there will be twelve hosts of gods, each consisting of one group;
their Indra, O twice-born one, will be of great heroism and wonderful.
Savana, Dyutimān, Bhavya, Vasu, Medhādhṛti, Jyotiṣmān as the seventh, and Satya; these were the great seers there. || 22 ||
Dhṛtaketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya,
Pṛthuśravas, and others were likewise the sons of Dakṣasāvarṇa.
O Sage, Daśama Brahmāsāvarṇi will be the Manu;
likewise, there will be one hundred gods known as the Sudhāmans and the Viruddhas.
Their Indra will be the very powerful one named Śānti;
and those who will be the seven ṛṣis at that time—listen to them as well: || 25 ||
Haviṣmān, Sukṛti, Satya, and likewise Apāmūrti; Nābhāga of incomparable prowess, and likewise Satyaketu. (26)
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, Hariṣeṇa, and the other ten sons of Brahmāsāvarṇi shall protect the earth. || 27 ||
And the eleventh Manu will be Dharmasāvarṇika;
[the gods] will be the Vihaṅgamas, the Kāmagamas, and likewise the Nirmāṇaratis.
These shall then be the principal hosts of the future gods;
each of their groups consists of thirty, and their Indras shall indeed be Vṛṣa. || 29 ||
Niścara, Agnitejas, Vapuṣmat, Viṣṇu, Āruṇi, Haviṣmat, and Anagha—these shall likewise be the seven ṛṣis. || 30 ||
Sarvaga, Sarvadharmā, Devānīka, and others likewise shall be his sons, lords of the earth, who will possess minds [intent on dharma]. || 31 ||
The twelfth Manu will be Sāvarṇa, the son of Rudra; Ṛtadhāman will be the Indra there; hear from me the names of the gods: || 32 ||
The Haritas, the Lohitas, the Devas, as well as the Sumanasas, O twice-born one, the Sukarmans, and the Tārakas—these indeed are the five groups of ten. || 33 ||
Tapasvin, Sutapas, Tapomūrti, Taporati, Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and another, the seventh, was Tapodhana.
Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and others likewise—these sons of that Manu shall be kings of great prowess. || 35 ||
O Sage, the thirteenth Manu will be named Raucya; his sons will be the Sutrāmaṇas, the Sudharmāṇas, and others known as the Sukarmāṇas.
Those hosts of gods consist of thirty-three divisions;
among them, the very powerful Divaspati shall become Indra. || 37 ||
The seventh son was the sage Sutapas, who was free from delusion, a seer of reality, unshakable, devoid of worldly longing, steadfast, and imperishable. || 38 ||
These are the seven ṛṣis; now learn from me also of his sons, who will be kings beginning with Citrasena and Vicitra. || 39 ||
O Maitreya, Bhautya shall be the fourteenth Manu here;
Śuci will be the Indra, and there will be five groups of gods; hear of them: || 40 ||
The Cākṣuṣas, the Pavitras, the Kanīṣṭhas, the Bhājiras, and the Vacovṛddhas were indeed the gods; now hear from me also about the seven Ṛṣis. || 41 ||
Agnibāhu, Śuci, Śukra, Māgadha, Agnīdhra, Yukta, and likewise Jita were others; now hear of the sons of Manu from him. || 42 ||
Urur, Gabhīra, Bradhna, and others—these sons of that Manu, O tiger among lords of sages, have been described as the kings who shall protect the earth. || 43 ||
At the end of the four yugas, it is said that the dissolution of the Vedas occurs;
then the seven ṛṣis, descending from heaven, cause them to be promulgated once again on earth.
O Brahmin, at the completion of each *kṛta* age, a Manu is born as the ordainer of memory;
those gods are the partakers of the sacrifice for as long as that *manvantara* lasts. || 45 ||
For as long as the Manvantara lasts, those who are the sons of Manu, as well as those born of their lineage, protect the earth. || 46 ||
In each Manvantara, Manu, the seven ṛṣis, the gods, and the sons of Manu—the kings—come into being, as does Śakra, who holds authority. || 47 ||
O twice-born one, when these fourteen Manvantaras have passed, a Kalpa, which consists of a thousand Yugas, is said to be complete without remainder. || 48 ||
O best of beings, the night thereafter is of that same duration;
assuming the form of Brahmā, he lies upon the serpent Śeṣa amidst the flood of waters.
O Brahmin, having swallowed the entire triple world, the Lord, the primordial creator, the all-pervading Janārdana, remains established in his own māyā, being the soul of all beings.
Then the Blessed One, awakened as before, the imperishable Self characterized by the quality of passion (rajas), brings about creation again in every kalpa. || 51 ||
O best of the twice-born, the Manus, the kings, the gods including Indra, and likewise the seven ṛṣis, are the sāttvika portion that maintains the stability of the world.
O Maitreya, listen to how that Viṣṇu, whose characteristic is the activity of preservation, establishes the order of the ages throughout the four yugas! || 53 ||
In the Kṛta age, he who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, assuming the form of Kapila and others, bestows supreme knowledge upon all living creatures.
In the Tretā age as well, that Lord, assuming the form of a universal monarch (cakravartin), protects the three worlds while subduing the wicked. || 55 ||
Having divided this single Veda into four parts and further into hundreds of branches, the omnipresent Lord, assuming the form of Vedavyāsa, makes it manifold once again. || 56 ||
Having divided the Vedas during the Dvāpara age, the Lord Hari, at the end of the Kali age, assumes the form of Kalki and establishes those of evil conduct on the right path. || 57 ||
Thus this infinite Self protects and creates this entire world, and at the end he destroys it; there is nothing that exists apart from him.
O Brahmin, the true nature of all great-souled beings— of those that have been, those that are, and those that will be— has been described to you here or elsewhere.
All the Manvantaras have been recounted by me to you, as well as the lords of those Manvantaras; what else shall I tell you? || 60 ||
